overview: This unit covers the empty set (leere Menge), the universal set (Grundmenge; Universum), Karnaugh–Veitch diagrams (KV-Diagramme), set terms (Mengenterme), and set identities (Mengenidentitäten). It distinguishes sets from sequences (Folgen) and tuples (Tupel), and introduces membership patterns (Mitgliedschaftsmuster), Gray order (Gray-Reihenfolge), truth tables for set identities (Wahrheitstabellen für Mengenidentitäten), index sets (Indexmengen), sequence terms (Folgeglieder), cardinality (Mächtigkeit), and Cartesian products (kartesische Produkte), including products with multiple factors (Produkte mit mehreren Faktoren) and empty products (leere Produkte). It also covers empty tuples (leere Tupel), geometric sequences (geometrische Folgen), alphabets (Alphabete), words (Wörter), word length (Wortlänge), formal languages (formale Sprachen), the empty word (leeres Wort), and word and language concatenation (Konkatenation von Wörtern und Sprachen).

entries.short: The empty set ∅ contains no elements.
entries.explanation: It holds that $|\varnothing|=0$. By contrast, $\{\varnothing\}$ contains the empty set as its only element and has cardinality 1. Thus, $\varnothing\ne\{\varnothing\}$.
entries.example: $\varnothing$ contains no elements, whereas $\{\varnothing\}$ contains the element $\varnothing$.
pitfalls: The empty set is not the set whose sole element is the empty set.
entries.heading: Rückblick: leere Menge und Grundmenge

entries.short: The universal set Ω specifies which elements are considered when working with sets.
entries.explanation: The complement of a set $A\subseteq\Omega$ consists of the elements of $\Omega$ that are not in $A$. Therefore, a universal set must be specified for the complement to be uniquely determined. The complement of $\varnothing$ relative to $\Omega$ is $\Omega$.
pitfalls: Without a specified universal set, a complement is not uniquely determined.
entries.heading: Rückblick: leere Menge und Grundmenge

entries.short: A KV diagram arranges all membership cases so that neighboring cells differ in exactly one bit.
entries.explanation: For $n$ sets, there are $2^n$ membership cases and therefore $2^n$ cells. One bit represents one set; 1 indicates membership and 0 indicates nonmembership. To extend the diagram, reflect the existing diagram and mark the new set as an additional bit. Opposite outer edges are also considered adjacent.
entries.example: For three sets, there are $2^3=8$ cells, one for each bit string of length 3.
pitfalls: The cells must be ordered so that neighboring cells differ in only one bit.
When checking adjacency, include opposite outer edges.
entries.heading: KV-Diagramme durch Spiegeln aufbauen

entries.short: A set identity states that two set terms have the same result for every permitted assignment of their set variables.
entries.explanation: The symbol $=$ can denote, among other things, a definition, an equality after evaluation, or an equation with an unknown set. An identity holds independently of the particular assignment; the symbol $\equiv$ emphasizes this semantic equivalence. The symbol $:=$ can be used for a definition.
entries.example: $X\cup Y\equiv Y\cup X$ is an identity, whereas $\{5\}\cup\{6\}=\{5,6\}$ is an equality after evaluation.
pitfalls: An equality for particular sets is not automatically an identity.
Syntactically different terms can have the same result for every assignment.
entries.heading: Was bedeutet Gleichheit bei Mengentermen?

entries.short: A truth table compares membership in two set terms for every possible membership case.
entries.explanation: For an arbitrary element, record its membership in the sets under consideration as 0 or 1. Evaluate both terms for each of these bit assignments. If their result columns agree in every row, the identity holds.
entries.example: For $A\cap(B\cup C)$ and $(A\cap B)\cup(A\cap C)$, the result columns agree for all eight assignments of A, B, and C.
pitfalls: If a row is omitted, a counterexample may be missed.
entries.heading: Distributivgesetz durch eine Wahrheitstabelle zeigen

entries.term: Number of possible result patterns of set terms (Anzahl möglicher Ergebnismuster von Mengentermen)
entries.short: For n sets, there are $2^{2^n}$ possible result patterns over the membership cases.
entries.explanation: For $n$ sets, there are $2^n$ membership cases. A result pattern specifies for each case whether an element belongs to the resulting set, so there are $2^{2^n}$ patterns. For three sets, this is $2^8=256$ patterns; for four sets, it is $2^{16}=65\,536$. This number counts possible truth tables, not syntactic terms.
entries.example: For three sets, the eight membership cases can be marked as included or not included in 256 ways.
pitfalls: For particular fixed sets, fewer result patterns may occur if some membership cases are empty.
There are infinitely many syntactic set terms, even though only finitely many result patterns are possible.
entries.heading: Wie viele unterschiedliche Mengenterme gibt es?

entries.short: Set identities allow equivalent transformations regardless of the particular assignment of the set variables.
entries.explanation: Basic laws include idempotence $A\cup A\equiv A$, the identity element $A\cup\varnothing\equiv A$, commutativity $A\cup B\equiv B\cup A$, and associativity $(A\cup B)\cup C\equiv A\cup(B\cup C)$. The distributive law is $A\cap(B\cup C)\equiv(A\cap B)\cup(A\cap C)$. Since these identities hold for all sets, their variables can be replaced with arbitrary set terms.
entries.example: Substituting $P\setminus Q$ and $R$ into the commutativity law yields $(P\setminus Q)\cup R\equiv R\cup(P\setminus Q)$.
pitfalls: In a transformation, the parentheses and the law being applied must be consistent.
entries.heading: Wichtige Mengenidentitäten

entries.short: For a set, order and repetition do not matter; for a sequence, both matter.
entries.explanation: A set specifies which elements it contains; the order in which they are listed does not change the set, and repetitions are not counted more than once. A sequence is ordered and preserves each occurrence at its position. Sets are written with braces and sequences with parentheses.
pitfalls: Changing the order in a set listing does not create a new set.
Repetitions must not be removed from a sequence.
entries.heading: Mengen, Folgen und Tupel

entries.short: A sequence assigns an object to each index, and a finite sequence is also called a tuple.
entries.explanation: A sequence is specified by its entries and their corresponding indices. Its entries are read in increasing index order, preserving both order and repetitions. A finite sequence is written as a tuple.
entries.example: For the index set $[3]=\{1,2,3\}$, the sequence is $(a_i)_{i\in[3]}=(a_1,a_2,a_3)$.
pitfalls: A tuple with its entries swapped is generally a different tuple.
entries.heading: Mengen, Folgen und Tupel

entries.short: The notation $(a_i)_{i\in I}$ denotes the sequence of its entries ordered by index.
entries.explanation: The index set is a subset of $\mathbb N_0$; common choices include $I=\mathbb N$, $I=\mathbb N_0$, or $I=[n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}$. The object $a_i$ is called the ith sequence term, entry, or component. For a finite sequence, its length is the cardinality of its index set: $\bigl|(a_i)_{i\in I}\bigr|:=|I|$.
pitfalls: Indexing can begin at 0 or 1; the specified index set determines which convention applies.
entries.heading: Indexmenge und Folgeglieder

entries.short: The empty tuple () is the sequence with no entries and has length 0.
entries.explanation: For the empty index set, we obtain $(a_i)_{i\in\varnothing}=()$. Its length is $|()|=0$. The empty tuple is a single object and must not be confused with the empty set.
entries.example: The product with zero factors is $\{()\}$: a set with one element, namely the empty tuple.
pitfalls: The empty tuple has length 0, whereas the set $\{()\}$ has cardinality 1.
entries.heading: Indexmenge und Folgeglieder

entries.short: A geometric sequence has terms of the form $a_i=cq^i$ for fixed $c,q\in\mathbb R$.
entries.explanation: For fixed real numbers $c$ and $q$, each sequence term is specified by $a_i=cq^i$. At consecutive indices, each term is obtained by multiplying the previous one by $q$. The index set used determines the starting index.
pitfalls: The starting index is part of the sequence's specification.
entries.heading: Genannte Folgen und Reihen

entries.short: The Cartesian product $A\times B$ consists of ordered pairs whose first component is from A and whose second component is from B.
entries.explanation: Formally, $A\times B:=\{(a,b)\mid a\in A,\ b\in B\}$. The parentheses denote an ordered pair. The Cartesian product itself is a set of such pairs.
pitfalls: The order of the components is part of the pair.
entries.heading: Kartesisches Produkt: Mengen geordneter Tupel

entries.short: For finite sets, $|A\times B|=|A|\cdot|B|$.
entries.explanation: For each of the $|A|$ possible first components, there are $|B|$ possible second components. Thus, there are $|A|\cdot|B|$ ordered pairs in total. If either set is empty, the product is empty and the formula still holds.
pitfalls: Here the formula uses finite cardinalities as natural numbers.
entries.heading: Alle Kombinationen als Tabelle

entries.short: The product $A_1\times\cdots\times A_k$ contains the k-tuples whose ith component comes from $A_i$.
entries.explanation: Formally, $A_1\times\cdots\times A_k:=\{(a_i)_{i\in[k]}\mid a_i\in A_i\text{ für alle }i\in[k]\}$, where $[k]=\{1,\ldots,k\}$. With one factor, the product formally contains 1-tuples; identifying these with the elements themselves would need to be agreed upon. If all factors are A, write $A^k$; in particular, $\mathbb R^2=\mathbb R\times\mathbb R$.
pitfalls: The product with one factor formally consists of 1-tuples.
entries.heading: Mehrere Faktoren, ein Faktor und kein Faktor

entries.short: The Cartesian product with zero factors is the set $\{()\}$, whose only element is the empty tuple.
entries.explanation: The convention is $\mathop{\Large\times}_{i=1}^{0}A_i=\{()\}$. The empty tuple has length 0, but the set $\{()\}$ has one element. This allows product rules to be stated uniformly, including for zero factors.
pitfalls: The empty product is not the empty set.
The empty tuple has length 0, whereas the cardinality of $\{()\}$ is 1.
entries.heading: Mehrere Faktoren, ein Faktor und kein Faktor

entries.term: Distributive laws of the Cartesian product (Distributivgesetze des kartesischen Produkts)
entries.short: The Cartesian product with A distributes over union, intersection, and set difference in the second factor.
entries.explanation: The laws $A\times(B\cup C)=(A\times B)\cup(A\times C)$, $A\times(B\cap C)=(A\times B)\cap(A\times C)$, and $A\times(B\setminus C)=(A\times B)\setminus(A\times C)$ hold. In each case, the first component must belong to A. The condition on the second component follows from the set operation.
entries.example: A pair $(a,b)$ belongs to $A\times(B\cup C)$ exactly when $a\in A$ and either $b\in B$ or $b\in C$.
pitfalls: For set difference, the second component must belong to B and not to C.
entries.heading: Distributivgesetze und Reihenfolge

entries.term: Order of components in a Cartesian product (Reihenfolge im kartesischen Produkt)
entries.short: The Cartesian product is generally not commutative because an ordered pair distinguishes its first and second components.
entries.explanation: In general, $A\times B\ne B\times A$, because swapping the components can produce different ordered pairs. For example, $(1,2)$ and $(2,1)$ are distinct. However, there are special cases in which the products are equal, such as when both are empty.
pitfalls: The fact that A and B differ does not by itself guarantee that the products differ.
entries.heading: Distributivgesetze und Reihenfolge

entries.short: An alphabet Σ is a nonempty set of symbols treated as indivisible units.
entries.explanation: The symbols of an alphabet are the building blocks from which words are formed. An alphabet is often finite. If a symbol visibly consists of several letters, its notation must make its boundaries unambiguous.
entries.example: $\Sigma=\{a,b\}$ is an alphabet with two symbols.
pitfalls: A string of visible letters can be ambiguous if the symbol boundaries are not specified.
entries.heading: Alphabete und Wörter

entries.short: A word over Σ is a finite sequence of symbols from the alphabet Σ.
entries.explanation: A tuple $(a_1,\ldots,a_n)\in\Sigma^n$ can be written as the word $a_1a_2\cdots a_n$ if the individual symbols are unambiguous. Their order and all repetitions are preserved. Bit strings are words over the alphabet $\{0,1\}$.
pitfalls: Writing a word without commas is unambiguous only when the symbol boundaries are clear.
entries.heading: Alphabete und Wörter

entries.short: The length of a word is the number of its symbols and is denoted by $|w|$.
entries.explanation: For a word $w=(a_1,\ldots,a_n)$, $|w|=n$. Order affects the word, but not its length. The empty word has length 0.
pitfalls: Count symbols according to the specified alphabet, which need not correspond to the visible letters.
entries.heading: Alphabete und Wörter

entries.short: $\Sigma^n$ denotes the words of length n over Σ, and $\Sigma^*$ contains all finite words over Σ.
entries.explanation: For $n\in\mathbb N_0$, $\Sigma^n$ is the set of all n-tuples of symbols from Σ, read as words. In particular, $\Sigma^0=\{\varepsilon\}$. Also, $\Sigma^*:=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N_0}\Sigma^n$.
pitfalls: $\Sigma^*$ also contains the empty word.
entries.heading: Meine Eselsbrücke zu formalen Sprachen

entries.short: A formal language over Σ is a subset of $\Sigma^*$.
entries.explanation: Since $\Sigma^*$ contains all finite words over the alphabet Σ, a language $L\subseteq\Sigma^*$ specifies which words belong to it. Its elements are words, not individual symbols. For each word, whether it belongs to L is uniquely determined.
entries.example: For $\Sigma=\{a,b\}$, $L=\{\varepsilon,\mathtt a,\mathtt{ab}\}$ is a language; $\mathtt{ba}\notin L$.
pitfalls: A language consists of words over the alphabet, not individual alphabet symbols.
entries.heading: Meine Eselsbrücke zu formalen Sprachen

entries.short: The empty word ε is the word of length 0 and corresponds to the empty tuple.
entries.explanation: It holds that $\varepsilon=()$, $|\varepsilon|=0$, and $\Sigma^0=\{\varepsilon\}$. The empty word contains no symbols, but it is itself a word and belongs to $\Sigma^*$. It is the identity element for concatenation.
pitfalls: The empty word is not the empty language $\varnothing$; $\{\varepsilon\}$ is a language containing exactly one word.
entries.heading: Meine Eselsbrücke zu formalen Sprachen

entries.short: Concatenation uv appends the symbols of v directly after the symbols of u.
entries.explanation: If $u=(u_1,\ldots,u_m)$ and $v=(v_1,\ldots,v_n)$, then $uv=(u_1,\ldots,u_m,v_1,\ldots,v_n)$. Concatenation is associative, the empty word is its identity element, and lengths add: $u(vw)=(uv)w$, $u\varepsilon=\varepsilon u=u$, and $|uv|=|u|+|v|$. In general, concatenation is not commutative.
pitfalls: Swapping the words can change the result.
entries.heading: Konkatenation: Wörter hintereinanderhängen

entries.short: The concatenation UV contains all words uv with $u\in U$ and $v\in V$.
entries.explanation: Formally, $UV:=\{uv\mid u\in U,\ v\in V\}$. This combines one word from U with one from V, in that order. The result is again a set of words.
entries.example: For $U=\{\mathtt a,\mathtt b\}$ and $V=\{\varepsilon,\mathtt a\}$, $UV=\{\mathtt a,\mathtt{aa},\mathtt b,\mathtt{ba}\}$.
pitfalls: UV is a set of words, not a single word.
entries.heading: Konkatenation ganzer Sprachen
